The father is himself the captive, not his daughter. He is being held by a kidnapper/captor, and the smartphone call is arranged so he can speak with his daughter; she pleads over the phone for his life to be spared. The captor shouts the demand—one hundred million yen, brought alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage dies, no police—but the hostage whose life is threatened is the father. The father also knows (from understanding his captor's intentions) that the captor will in any case kill him regardless of whether the money is paid; the captor has no intention of honoring the bargain. Therefore the father decides the ransom should not be paid: paying would not save his own life, because the threat to him is not conditional on the money. It would only give the captor the money. His refusal is thus a rational judgment based on his knowledge that the captor will kill him regardless—not indifference to a daughter genuinely in danger and not a denial that a real hostage exists.
